lesson.title: Bubbles as Proof: Gas Evolution Reactions
lesson.summary: A gas evolution reaction is a double replacement reaction whose products include a gas that escapes the solution, which is what drives the reaction forward and what you see as bubbling.
lesson.body:
Recall the double replacement pattern: two aqueous compounds swap partners, and the reaction only proceeds noticeably if one of the new combinations removes ions from solution, either as an insoluble precipitate, a weak electrolyte, or, in this case, a gas. Recall too that gases are far less dense and far more mobile than liquids, which lets a gas product simply leave the reaction mixture entirely, escaping into the air as bubbles. Once a product physically leaves the system, it can no longer take part in any reverse reaction, and that removal is exactly what pulls the overall reaction forward, in much the same way a precipitate falling out of solution drives a precipitation reaction to completion.

Many gas evolution reactions proceed through an unstable intermediate compound that decomposes into water plus a gas almost as soon as it forms. Carbonic acid, H2CO3, is the most common example, breaking down into H2O and CO2 gas. Ammonium hydroxide behaves similarly, decomposing into H2O and NH3 gas. Other common gases produced this way include SO2 and H2S.

Here is a fully worked, verified example: sodium sulfide reacting with hydrochloric acid, Na2S(aq) + 2HCl(aq) is right arrow 2NaCl(aq) + H2S(g). Check the atoms: sodium, 2 on each side. Sulfur, 1 on each side. Hydrogen, 2 on the left from 2HCl, matching 2 on the right in H2S. Chlorine, 2 on each side. The equation is balanced, and the unmistakable rotten egg smell of H2S escaping is your direct evidence that the reaction happened. Worth pointing out explicitly: this is not a redox reaction. Check the oxidation numbers if you like, sodium stays +1, sulfur stays -2, hydrogen stays +1, and chlorine stays -1, on both sides of the equation. Nothing is oxidized or reduced here. Gas evolution reactions and redox reactions are two separate categories of chemical reaction, and it is worth keeping them distinct even though you are studying both in the same unit.

The single most common and recognizable gas evolution reaction involves acids reacting with carbonates, a pattern common enough, and useful enough as a diagnostic test, to deserve its own dedicated look next.
